definitions.text: Being only one of a larger population; single, individual.
examples: Synonyms: individual; see also Thesaurus:specific
Antonyms: general; see also Thesaurus:generic
A singular experiment cannot be regarded as scientific proof of the existence of a phenomenon.
And God forbid that all a company / Should rue a singular manne's folly.And may God forbid that a whole group should suffer for a single man's folly.
And may God forbid that a whole group should suffer for a single man's folly.

definitions.text: Being the only one of the kind; unique.
examples: Synonyms: unique; see also Thesaurus:unique
She has a singular personality.
The busts […] of the emperors and empresses are all very scarce, and some of them almost singular in their kind.
singular instances
A group of finches, of which Mr. Gould considers there are thirteen species; and these he has distributed into for new sub-genera. These birds are the most singular of any in the archipelago.

definitions.text: Distinguished by superiority: peerless, unmatched, eminent, exceptional, extraordinary.
examples: Synonyms: exceptional, extraordinary, remarkable
a man of singular gravity or attainments

definitions.text: Out of the ordinary; curious.
examples: Synonyms: curious, eccentric, funny, odd, peculiar, rum, rummy, strange, unusual; see also Thesaurus:strange
It was very singular; I don't know why he did it.
So ſingular a ſadneſs / Muſt have a cauſe as ſtrange as the effect: […]
His zeal / None seconded, as out of season judged, / Or singular and rash.

definitions.text: Referring to only one thing or person.
examples: Antonym: plural

definitions.text: Having no inverse.
examples: Synonym: non-invertible
Antonyms: invertible, non-singular

definitions.text: Having the property that the matrix of coefficients of the new variables has a determinant equal to zero.
Not equal to its own cofinality.
Each; individual.
examples: to convey several parcels of land, all and singular

Cel[adon]. […] Hovv do Meliſſa’s tvvo fair Daughters? / Aſt[eria]. VVhen you tell me vvhich of ’em you are in love vvith, I’le anſvver you. / Cel. VVhich of ’em, naughty ſiſter, vvhat a question’s there? VVith both of ’em, vvith each and singular of ’em.

definitions.text: Engaged in by only one on a side; single.
examples: Thus made he an end, and the two princes allowed well of his last motion, and so order was taken, that they should fight togither in a singular combat

definitions.text: A form of a word that refers to only one person or thing.
examples: Antonym: plural

definitions.text: That which is not general; a specific determinate instance.
A group of boars.
examples: He rode as it were mechanically forward with his late counsellors, Diego and Gonsalez, at his side; and though, when "a singular of boars" was hunted out from his covert by the fierce Alauntes, the king followed up the chase, and even threw a spear at the bristled animal, yet it was with little spirit, and so ill aimed that the spear struck, and broke short, against an ancient oak tree of the forest.

The harts and hinds in their herds, the boars in their singulars, the skulls of foxes, the richesses of martens, the bevies of roes, the cetes of badgers and the routs of wolves - all came to him more or less as something which you either skinned or flayed and then took home to cook.

definitions.text: Relating to now, for the time being; current.
examples: The barbaric practice continues to the present day.
The present manager has been here longer than the last one.
up to the present day

All this was extraordinarily distasteful to Churchill. It was ugly, gross. Never before had he felt such repulsion when the vicar displayed his characteristic bluntness or coarseness of speech. In the present connexion […] such talk had been distressingly out of place.

definitions.text: Located in the immediate vicinity.
examples: Only half of all present members were present at the meeting.
Is there a doctor present?
Several people were present when the event took place.
Being the leader, Jason is always present at class.

definitions.text: Having an immediate effect (of a medicine, poison etc.); fast-acting. [16th–18th c.]
examples: Amongſt this number of Cordials and Alteratiues, J doe not find a more preſent remedy, then a cup of wine, or ſtrong drinke, and if it be ſoberly and opportunely vſed.

definitions.text: Not delayed; immediate; instant.
examples: Sign me a present pardon for my brother,
An ambassador […] desires a present audience.

definitions.text: Ready; quick in emergency.
examples: a present wit

definitions.text: Favorably attentive; propitious.
examples: to find a god so present to my prayer

definitions.text: Relating to something a person is referring to in the very context, with a deictic use similar to the demonstrative adjective this.
examples: Near-synonyms: this (determiner), this (pronoun), current
in the present study; the present article; the present results

definitions.text: Attentive; alert; focused.
examples: Sorry, I was distracted just now, I'll try to be more present from now on.

definitions.text: Neither for or against (used in voting to express abstention)
The current moment or period of time.
The present tense.
A gift, especially one given for birthdays, Christmas, anniversaries, graduations, weddings, or any other special occasions.
examples: wedding present; birthday present
wedding present
birthday present
Oh! Thank you for the presents! How considerate of you!
Only his friends attended his birthday party. They're all broke, so he got no present.

“A very welcome, kind, useful present, that means to the parish. By the way, Hopkins, let this go no further. We don't want the tale running round that a rich person has arrived. Churchill, my dear fellow, we have such greedy sharks, and wolves in lamb's clothing. […]”

definitions.text: The position of a soldier in presenting arms.
examples: The platoon stands at present.
He was at present near the headquarters gates.

definitions.text: Poo; feces.
examples: I think our toddler's just left us a little present in his diaper...
She has to deal with her cats' presents in the litterboxes on a daily basis, and she doesn't mind one bit.

definitions.text: To bring (someone) into the presence of (a person); to introduce formally. [from 14th c.]
examples: to present an envoy to the king

definitions.text: To appear or represent oneself outwardly.
examples: With your shabby attire, you do not present well as a prospective investment banking associate!

definitions.text: To nominate (a member of the clergy) for an ecclesiastical benefice; to offer to the bishop or ordinary as a candidate for institution. [from 14th c.]
To offer (a problem, complaint) to a court or other authority for consideration. [from 14th c.]
To charge (a person) with a crime or accusation; to bring before court. [from 14th c.]
examples: In the diocese of Gloucester in 1548 two inhabitants of Slimbridge were presented for saying that holy oil was ‘of no virtue but meet to grease sheep’.

definitions.text: To come forward, appear in a particular place or before a particular person, especially formally. [from 14th c.]
examples: Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the lord.

definitions.text: To put (something) forward in order for it to be seen; to show, exhibit. [from 14th c.]
examples: So ladies in romance assist their knight, / Present the spear, and arm him for the fight.
Note: The offensive team must present a legal formation both before and after a shift.

definitions.text: To make clear to one's mind or intelligence; to put forward for consideration. [from 14th c.]
examples: I do begin to realize that the matter must be presented in such a way as may interest the reader.

Libertarian paternalism is the view that, because the way options are presented to citizens affects what they choose, society should present options in a way that “nudges” our intuitive selves to make choices that are more consistent with what our more deliberative selves would have chosen if they were in control.

definitions.text: To put on, stage (a play etc.). [from 16th c.]
examples: The theater is proud to present the Fearless Fliers.

definitions.text: To point (a firearm) at something, to hold (a weapon) in a position ready to fire. [from 16th c.]
To offer oneself for mental consideration; to occur to the mind. [from 16th c.]
examples: Well, one idea does present itself.

definitions.text: To come to the attention of medical staff, especially with a specific symptom. [from 19th c.]
examples: The patient presented with insomnia.
Symptoms typically present in early childhood.

definitions.text: To appear (in a specific way) for delivery (of a fetus); to appear first at the mouth of the uterus during childbirth. [from 18th c.]
To appear or represent oneself (as having a certain gender).
examples: At that time, Elbe was presenting as a man.

In May 2019, a case was referred to the high court in which social workers for Lancashire county council had sought orders against the parents of two trans children to take the children into care. Social services were alerted when H, the couple’s three-year-old foster child, born male, had gone into school presenting as a girl.

definitions.text: To act as presenter on (a radio, television programme etc.). [from 20th c.]
examples: Anne Robinson presents "The Weakest Link".

definitions.text: To give a gift or presentation to (someone). [from 14th c.]
examples: Synonyms: compliment, bestow
She was presented with an honorary degree for her services to entertainment.
Live thou, and reign, forever, glorious Lord! / My last, least off’ring, I present thee now— / Renounce me, leave me, and be still ador’d! / Slay me, my God, and I applaud the blow.

definitions.text: To deliver (something abstract) as though as a gift; to offer. [from 14th c.]
examples: I presented my compliments to Lady Featherstoneshaw.

definitions.text: To hand over (a bill etc.) to be paid. [from 15th c.]
To display one's female genitalia in a way that signals to others that one is ready for copulation. Also referred to as lordosis behaviour. [from 20th c.]
In omegaverse fiction, to have one's secondary sex (alpha, omega, or beta) become apparent, typically at puberty. [from 21st c.]
examples: Sherlock’s gender performance itself remains unchanged, with the exception of the hormonal changes he goes through after presenting as an omega.
People “present” their secondary genders during puberty, so girls and boys are raised without knowing if they will be alphas, betas, or omegas.

definitions.text: Serving as a sign, indication or suggestion of something.
examples: He had pains indicative of a heart attack.

Although it may be convenient within the case study publication format to cover the topic of pseudopathology in the discussion of differential diagnosis, this is not indicative of how this stage of work slots into the diagnostic process in the laboratory.

definitions.text: Of, or relating to the indicative mood.
The indicative mood.
A term in the indicative mood.
examples: The fact that imperative forms were taken into English as indicatives suggests that the English speakers using the Hindustani verbs were most familiar (in some cases perhaps only familiar) with the imperative form.

definitions.text: To damage beyond use or repair; to damage (something) to the point that it effectively ceases to exist.
examples: The earthquake destroyed several apartment complexes.
Hooligans destroy unprovoked.
Iesus answered, and said vnto them, Destroy this temple, and in three dayes I will raise it vp.

Repeated use of this type of [water] on plants results in deflocculation[] of the soil. Good quality soil consists of loose aggregates which provide natural aeration and ease of root run. Sodium accumulation in soil destroys this natural flocculation and causes the soil to pack.
Krav is a martial art of last resort that assumes no quarter and focuses purely on disarming, disabling and, if necessary, destroying your opponent.

Musk’s Israel tour was transparently transactional and frankly insulting. The antisemitic sentiment Musk endorsed had nothing to do with Israel; “replacement theory” is generally an unsupported allegation that Jews and other immigrants in the US and Europe are destroying Western civilization.

definitions.text: To neutralize, undo a property or condition.
examples: Smoking destroys the natural subtlety of the palate.

definitions.text: To put down or euthanize.
examples: Destroying a rabid dog is required by law.

definitions.text: To severely disrupt the well-being of (a person); ruin.
examples: Her divorce destroyed her; she had a nervous breakdown and was severely depressed for more than a year.
Other girls in the foster home are eager to destroy her and get her kicked out of the place. It's a tough situation.

definitions.text: To utterly defeat; to crush.
examples: Remember when Germany destroyed Brazil 7–1 in the World Cup?
Growing up, [Kevin] Durant told me, he was a sore loser. That all changed one day when he was 11, after he got destroyed by his father in a game of one on one in the driveway.

definitions.text: To remove data.
examples: The memory leak happened because we forgot to destroy the temporary lists.

definitions.text: To exhaust completely and thus recreate or build up.
examples: This exercise is going to destroy all parts of your shoulders.

definitions.text: To penetrate sexually in an aggressive way.
examples: She got destroyed by her lover on the carpet.

definitions.text: To sing a song extremely poorly.
examples: JAMES CARTER: The man's destroying a classic!

definitions.text: To eat food quickly, hungrily or completely.
examples: I could destroy some wings right now.

Pronunciation[edit] · English Wikipedia has an article on:presentWikipedia English Wikipedia has an article on:present present From Middle English present, from Old French present, from Latin praesent-, praesens, present participle of praeesse (“to be present”), from Latin prae- (“pre-”) + esse (“to be”). Displaced Old English andweard (“present, current”). Adjective[edit] From Middle English presenten, from Old French presenter, from Latin praesentāre (“to show”), from praesent-, praesens, present participle of praeesse (“be in front of”). Noun[edit] From presend + -t. Verb[edit] · From Middle French indicatif, from Late Latin indicātīvus. By surface analysis, indicate +‎ -ive. definitions.text: third-person singular simple present indicative of destroy
(ambitransitive) To damage beyond use or repair; to damage (something) to the point that it effectively ceases to exist.
examples: The earthquake destroyed several apartment complexes.
Hooligans destroy unprovoked.
Iesus answered, and said vnto them, Destroy this temple, and in three dayes I will raise it vp.

Repeated use of this type of [water] on plants results in deflocculation[] of the soil. Good quality soil consists of loose aggregates which provide natural aeration and ease of root run. Sodium accumulation in soil destroys this natural flocculation and causes the soil to pack.
Krav is a martial art of last resort that assumes no quarter and focuses purely on disarming, disabling and, if necessary, destroying your opponent.

Musk’s Israel tour was transparently transactional and frankly insulting. The antisemitic sentiment Musk endorsed had nothing to do with Israel; “replacement theory” is generally an unsupported allegation that Jews and other immigrants in the US and Europe are destroying Western civilization.

definitions.text: (transitive) To neutralize, undo a property or condition.
examples: Smoking destroys the natural subtlety of the palate.

definitions.text: (transitive) To put down or euthanize.
examples: Destroying a rabid dog is required by law.

definitions.text: (transitive) To severely disrupt the well-being of (a person); ruin.
examples: Her divorce destroyed her; she had a nervous breakdown and was severely depressed for more than a year.
Other girls in the foster home are eager to destroy her and get her kicked out of the place. It's a tough situation.

definitions.text: (transitive, informal) To utterly defeat; to crush.
examples: Remember when Germany destroyed Brazil 7–1 in the World Cup?
Growing up, [Kevin] Durant told me, he was a sore loser. That all changed one day when he was 11, after he got destroyed by his father in a game of one on one in the driveway.

definitions.text: (transitive, computing) To remove data.
examples: The memory leak happened because we forgot to destroy the temporary lists.

definitions.text: (transitive, bodybuilding, slang, antiphrasis) To exhaust completely and thus recreate or build up.
examples: This exercise is going to destroy all parts of your shoulders.

definitions.text: (transitive, slang, vulgar) To penetrate sexually in an aggressive way.
examples: She got destroyed by her lover on the carpet.

definitions.text: (transitive, US, slang) To sing a song extremely poorly.
examples: JAMES CARTER: The man's destroying a classic!

definitions.text: (transitive, slang) To eat food quickly, hungrily or completely.
examples: I could destroy some wings right now.
